title: Geostationary Satellite
short_intro: A geostationary satellite is an earth-orbiting satellite that has an orbital period equal to the earth's rotational period of 23 hours 56 minutes and 4 seconds. It appears stationary relative to a specific point on the earth's equator due to its synchronous prograde equatorial orbit.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, time period, orbital radius from the earth's surface, equatorial orbit condition, and basic applications in communication.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of orbital radius and velocity, energy considerations, stability criteria, perturbation effects due to solar-lunar gravitational forces, and parking orbit injection mechanics.

prerequisites: Centripetal Force and Central Force Motion
Kepler's Third Law of Planetary Motion

concept_notes.heading: Orbital Synchronicity and Period
bullets: The time period T of the satellite must exactly match the sidereal rotation period of the Earth, which is T = 86164 s.
The satellite must move in the same direction as the Earth's rotation (prograde motion).
The angular velocity of the satellite in its orbit must equal the angular velocity of the Earth about its spin axis, ω = 7.292 × 10<sup>-5</sup> rad/s.

concept_notes.heading: Equatorial Plane Requirement
bullets: The orbit must lie strictly in the plane of the Earth's equator (inclination i = 0<deg>).
If the orbit is inclined, the satellite will trace a figure-eight path in the sky daily, failing to remain stationary over a single geographic location.
Equatorial placement ensures that the line of sight from the ground station to the satellite maintains a fixed azimuth and elevation.

concept_notes.heading: Orbital Radius and Altitude
bullets: The orbital radius r is calculated from the center of the Earth, approximately equal to 42,164 km.
The height h above the Earth's surface is approximately 35,786 km, accounting for the mean equatorial radius of the Earth (R_e ≈ 6378 km).
This high altitude allows a single satellite to cover roughly 40% of the Earth's surface for continuous telecommunication.

concept_notes.heading: Perturbations and Station-Keeping
bullets: Non-uniform gravitational fields of the Earth (J_2 term), gravitational pulls from the Sun and Moon, and solar radiation pressure perturb the orbit.
Station-keeping thrusters must be fired periodically to counteract longitudinal and latitudinal drift caused by these perturbations.
Without station-keeping, inclination drifts by about 0.85<deg> per year.

derivations.title: Derivation of Geostationary Orbital Radius
derivations.conditions: Circular, equatorial, synchronous orbit around a spherically symmetric Earth.
steps: Equate the gravitational force providing the necessary centripetal force: \frac{GMm}{r^2} = m\omega^2 r
Express angular velocity in terms of the time period T: \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}
Substitute \omega into the force equation: \frac{GM}{r^2} = \left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 r
Rearrange to solve for the orbital radius r: r^3 = \frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}

derivations.title: Derivation of Orbital Velocity for Geostationary Orbit
derivations.conditions: Circular equatorial orbit at radius r.
steps: Start with the balance of gravitational and centripetal acceleration: \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{GM}{r^2}
Express orbital velocity v in terms of gravitational constant G, Earth mass M, and radius r: v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}
Alternatively, relate v to the angular velocity \omega and radius r: v = \omega r
Substitute numerical values for \omega and r to find the linear speed.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Potential Energy vs. Orbital Radius
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of effective potential energy U_eff(r) showing a minimum corresponding to stable circular orbit at the geostationary radius.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The minimum of the effective potential well denotes the radius where centripetal and gravitational forces balance, providing stable equilibrium for the geostationary orbit.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT to explain orbital stability under central forces.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ground Trace of Satellite (Inclined vs. Equatorial)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A world map projection showing a point for a true geostationary satellite (i = 0<deg>) and a figure-eight analemma for an inclined geosynchronous satellite (i > 0<deg>).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates why zero inclination is mandatory for a truly stationary position relative to the Earth's surface.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual TGT/PGT multiple-choice question on ground track behavior.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Signal Coverage Footprint (Zenith Angle vs. Latitude)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic diagram showing the Earth's curvature limiting line-of-sight communication beyond approximately 81<deg> latitude from a geostationary satellite.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Explains polar coverage gaps for geostationary satellites, necessitating polar or inclined orbits for high-latitude communication.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Applied physics application questions in communication satellite logistics.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the height of a geostationary satellite above the Earth's surface. Given: Radius of Earth R_e = 6400 km, Mass of Earth M = 6 \times 10^{24} kg, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} N m^2 kg^{-2}, and T = 24 hours.
solution_steps: Using formula r^3 = \frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}, substitute the values: r^3 = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times (86400)^2}{4 \times (3.1416)^2}.
Height h = r - R_e = 42200 km - 6400 km = 35800 km.

solved_numericals.question: Find the orbital velocity and the binding energy of a geostationary satellite of mass 500 kg. Take orbital radius r = 4.2 \times 10^7 m, M = 6 \times 10^{24} kg, and G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} N m^2 kg^{-2}.

What is the minimum extra velocity (impulse delta-v) that must be imparted to a satellite in a circular low earth orbit (radius R_e) to transfer it to a geostationary transfer orbit whose apogee is at the geostationary radius r_g = 7 R_e?
solution_steps: Semi-major axis of transfer ellipse a = \frac{R_e + r_g}{2} = \frac{R_e + 7R_e}{2} = 4R_e.

Velocity at perigee of transfer ellipse v_p = \sqrt{GM \left(\frac{2}{R_e} - \frac{1}{a}\right)} = \sqrt{GM \left(\frac{2}{R_e} - \frac{1}{4R_e}\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{7GM}{4R_e}} = \sqrt{\frac{7}{4}} v_1.

assumptions_and_limitations: The Earth is treated as a uniform sphere with spherically symmetric mass distribution, neglecting equatorial bulge (J_2 perturbation) in basic derivations.
Gravitational pull from third bodies (Sun and Moon) is neglected in introductory models but accounted for in long-term orbital station-keeping.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A geostationary satellite can be placed directly above any point on the Earth, such as the poles.
common_misconceptions.correct: Geostationary satellites can only remain stationary above points on the Earth's equator.
common_misconceptions.why: The gravitational central force must act toward the center of the Earth, constraining the orbit to lie in a plane passing through the Earth's center (the equatorial plane).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Geostationary and geosynchronous satellites are identical terms.
common_misconceptions.correct: All geostationary satellites are geosynchronous, but not all geosynchronous satellites are geostationary.
common_misconceptions.why: A geosynchronous satellite has a 24-hour period but may have an inclined or elliptical orbit, whereas a geostationary satellite must be in a circular, zero-inclination equatorial orbit.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A geostationary satellite experiences zero gravity because it is weightless.
common_misconceptions.correct: The satellite experiences normal Earth gravity at its altitude, which acts as the required centripetal force for its orbit.
common_misconceptions.why: Weightlessness in orbit is a consequence of free fall, not the absence of gravity.

quick_revision: Geostationary orbit is circular, equatorial, prograde, with T = 24 hours and altitude h ≈ 35,786 km.
Kepler's Third Law for Satellite: r^3 = \frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}
